title: Filling the low brackets
teaches: Why low-income years are worth using on purpose: Roth conversions and 0 percent gains up to the top of a bracket, how the two compete for the same space, and what filling saves over a lifetime

blocks.text: A couple stops work at 60 with $600,000 in a taxable account, $1.2 million in traditional 401(k)s and IRAs, and $200,000 in Roth accounts. They spend $80,000 a year and will claim $50,000 a year of Social Security at 67. The usual advice is to spend the taxable account first, then the pre-tax accounts, and leave the Roth for last. Followed to the letter, it gives them seven years with almost no federal income tax: they live on share sales, mostly basis and the rest gains in the 0 percent band.

It sounds ideal, and it is one of the most expensive mistakes in retirement planning. While they pay nothing, the $1.2 million in pre-tax accounts keeps growing. At 75 the law requires withdrawals from it every year, and by then it is over $2 million.[^rmd] Their first required withdrawal is about $88,000, on top of $50,000 of Social Security, and both rise from there. The brackets they left empty in their sixties are gone for good; the tax arrives later, at higher rates.

The alternative is to use the empty years on purpose: each year, move enough from the pre-tax accounts into a Roth, or take enough as income, to fill the 10 and 12 percent brackets. What follows works out how much to move, and what gets in the way.

Think of each year's low brackets as space that expires on 31 December. A couple's standard deduction is $32,200 of space taxed at 0 percent. The 10 and 12 percent brackets add another $100,800. Any ordinary income placed in that space costs at most 12 percent, and the space can't be carried into next year.

Two things want the space: Roth conversions and long-term gains. Gains are taxed at 0 percent only while they fit under the $98,900 line, and lesson 7 showed that ordinary income goes underneath and pushes them out. So a couple living on gains who also converts pays twice for the same space: 12 percent on the conversion, plus 15 percent on each dollar of gains pushed up. Guess, then see it.

blocks.caption: A married couple living on long-term gains from a taxable account converts some pre-tax money to a Roth. Above: the federal tax the conversion adds. Below: the rate on the next $1,000 converted. The dashed line is the top of the 12 percent bracket.
blocks.task: Guess, then try small and large gains

blocks.text: With no gains, a conversion's cost rises by the brackets alone: nothing for the first $32,200, then 10 percent, then 12, then 22. With $40,000 of gains, there is a stretch where each extra dollar converted costs 27 percent, even though the couple never leaves the 12 percent bracket. With large gains the stretch widens.

The choice between the two isn't obvious. Gains realised at 0 percent are gone for good: the basis is raised and those gains never pay tax.[^reset] A conversion moves money that will otherwise be taxed later, probably at 12 or 22 percent. Many plans do both and stop each where it starts costing 27 percent: realise gains up to the 0 percent line in years with little ordinary income, and convert to the top of the 12 percent bracket in years when gains are small.

The course's household model runs the couple from 60 to 95 with each strategy: spending, tax, required withdrawals, Social Security, and growth of 4 percent a year after inflation. Filling to the top of the 12 percent bracket means drawing or converting pre-tax money each year until ordinary taxable income reaches $100,800, spending what's needed and converting the rest.

blocks.caption: The same couple from 60 to 95 under three withdrawal plans, from the course's household model. Federal income tax only.

blocks.text: Leaving the low brackets empty costs this couple about $385,000 in federal tax over their lives. Filling to the top of 12 percent costs about $160,000, and leaves their heirs some $780,000 more after tax. Filling to the top of 22 percent pays more tax than filling to 12, because it pays 22 percent on dollars that would otherwise have come out at 12.

Before 65, though, this couple buys health insurance on the ACA marketplace, and its premium credits shrink as income rises. Filling to 12 percent here pushes them over the line at which credits stop, costing about $68,000 in premiums over five years. Filling still wins, but by less, and a plan that keeps income under the line until 65 and fills harder afterwards may do better. Lesson 11 takes this apart.

The right top is the rate you expect the money to pay later, counting everything. As in lesson 8, the calculation comes down to four things: how big required withdrawals will be at 75, how much Social Security will arrive and when, whether one spouse will be widowed and filing alone with half the brackets,[^widow] and whether heirs will inherit pre-tax money in their own peak earning years.

Running the model on other households gives a few rough rules. Filling the 12 percent bracket usually pays for anyone with pre-tax savings well above $500,000. Filling into 22 percent tends to pay mainly for pre-tax balances in the millions, or for a couple whose survivor will face single brackets for many years. Filling to 24 percent and beyond rarely pays outside very large estates. Branch T's lessons and the capstone let you try your own numbers.

A few details affect the timing. Convert early in the year if markets have fallen, since the same tax moves more shares. Count on Social Security taxation (lesson 12) once benefits start, which can make the next dollar cost 22 or 40 percent inside the 12 percent bracket. And plan in advance for 63 and 64, whose income sets Medicare premiums two years later (lesson 12).

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Low brackets left empty in early retirement can't be used later; required withdrawals arrive at 73 or 75 and fill them for you, at higher rates.
Roth conversions and 0 percent gains compete for the same space; mixing them can cost 27 percent inside the 12 percent bracket.
For the sample couple, filling to the top of 12 percent cut lifetime federal tax from about $385,000 to $160,000.
The right top is the rate the money would pay later, counting required withdrawals, Social Security and a surviving spouse.

blocks.caption: Six questions on filling the brackets
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why can living only on a taxable account in early retirement turn out expensive?
choices: The pre-tax accounts keep growing, and required withdrawals later fill the brackets at higher rates
Taxable accounts are taxed at 37 percent
The basis is lost after ten years
items.why: Years of near-zero income waste the low brackets, while the pre-tax balance grows into large required withdrawals at 73 or 75.

items.ask: A couple with no other income converts $100,000 to a Roth in 2026. What is the federal tax?
items.why: $32,200 is covered by the standard deduction; the remaining $67,800 is taxed at 10 and 12 percent.

items.ask: A couple has $40,000 of gains and is converting inside the 12 percent bracket. Why can the next dollar converted cost 27 percent?
choices: It is taxed at 12 percent and pushes a dollar of gains from 0 to 15 percent
The 12 percent bracket ends at the 0 percent gains line
items.why: Ordinary income goes underneath the gains, so each dollar converted moves a dollar of gains above the 0 percent line.

items.ask: What happens to gains realised in the 0 percent band?
choices: They are never taxed, because the basis rises to the sale price
They are taxed later when the money is spent
They are added to next year's income
items.why: Selling and buying back raises the basis, so those gains are permanently free of tax.

items.ask: For the sample couple, roughly how much federal tax did filling to the top of the 12 percent bracket save over their lives?
choices: Nothing; it only moved tax around
items.why: About $385,000 with the low brackets left empty against about $160,000 with them filled.

items.ask: Which makes filling into the 22 percent bracket more worthwhile?
choices: A pre-tax balance in the millions
items.why: Large pre-tax balances mean large required withdrawals later, which land in 22 percent or above anyway.

summary: **Low brackets expire every year.** Space left empty in a low-income year can't be used later.
**Spending taxable first can backfire.** The pre-tax accounts grow untouched into large required withdrawals at 73 or 75.
**Conversions and 0 percent gains compete.** Mixing them can cost 27 percent inside the 12 percent bracket.
**0 percent gains are gone for good.** Realising them raises the basis, so those gains never pay tax.
**Filling the 12 percent bracket usually pays.** The sample couple's lifetime federal tax fell from about $385,000 to $160,000.
**Filling higher depends on the later rate.** Large pre-tax balances and a likely survivor filing single favour 22 percent.
**Health credits are part of the price.** Before 65, filling can cost more in lost premium credits than in tax.

rmd.title: Required minimum distributions
rmd.text: From the age set by law, 73 for people born from 1951 to 1959 and 75 for those born in 1960 or later, a share of each pre-tax account must be withdrawn each year: the balance at the end of the previous year divided by a life-expectancy figure from the IRS's Uniform Lifetime Table, 24.6 at 75. Roth accounts have no required withdrawals during the owner's life.

reset.title: Selling to reset the basis
reset.text: To realise a gain at 0 percent, sell shares and buy them straight back. The wash-sale rule, which stops you claiming a loss if you buy back within 30 days, doesn't apply to gains. The new basis is the price paid on the day, so future gains are measured from there. It only helps in a taxable account; inside a 401(k) or IRA there is no basis to reset.

widow.title: The survivor's brackets
widow.text: After one spouse dies, the survivor files as a single person (after the year of death, unless there is a dependent child). A single filer's standard deduction and 10, 12, 22 and 24 percent brackets are exactly half a married couple's, while required withdrawals from the combined pre-tax accounts stay just as large and only the smaller of the two Social Security benefits stops.
